Article Title: A California barber taught himself stock trading and built a $19 million fortune; after his death, his family accused Morgan Stanley of financial elder abuse, and an appeals court has revived key clai
Article Text:
From barber to self-taught investor

Family raised concerns about his declining health

Why the lower court dismissed the case

Appeals court says profits do not settle the question

Maurice Voce spent decades learning the stock market on his own, building a $19 million fortune through stock-options trading while working as a barber. But in the final years of his life, as his family became concerned about his declining cognitive health, questions emerged about whether the financial professionals managing his investments were adequately protecting his interests. Now, more than a decade after his death at 93, a California appeals court has revived key claims brought by his family against Morgan Stanley and financial adviser John Privitelli.In an opinion filed on October 8, 2026, and certified for publication on October 29, the California Court of Appeal ruled that the family’s financial elder abuse claim and parts of its breach-of-fiduciary-duty case should not have been dismissed. The decision in 'DeVone v. Morgan Stanley & Co. LLC' sends the dispute back for further proceedings, although it does not establish that Morgan Stanley or the adviser committed wrongdoing.According to the court opinion, Voce began investing in the 1960s and trading stock options in the 1970s. He worked with financial adviser Joseph Privitelli in the 1980s, when the adviser was associated with Dean Witter Reynolds, a firm that later merged with Morgan Stanley.After Joseph Privitelli died in 1993, his son, John Privitelli, took over Voce’s investment accounts. Voce was 74 at the time. The adviser continued working with him until June 2012, shortly before Voce died in August that year.Over the decades, Voce accumulated a fortune worth approximately $19 million, which he left to his three children through a series of trusts. His Morgan Stanley accounts were valued at about $18 million at the time of his death.His investments included a portfolio focused on income-generating assets and a separate trading account used for buying and selling stock options. These included covered calls, which involve owning the underlying shares, and uncovered options, which can expose investors to significantly greater risks.The family’s lawsuit alleged that the options-trading strategy was unsuitable for Voce in the final phase of his life and that the adviser continued facilitating trades and collecting commissions despite concerns about his cognitive health.The court record describes growing concerns among Voce’s children and other relatives about his memory and mental condition beginning around 2010. In December that year, family members emailed Privitelli about Voce’s memory lapses, disorientation and declining health. According to the appellate opinion, Privitelli acknowledged that he was aware of concerns about Voce’s cognitive impairment in early 2011, while continuing to execute trades based on Voce’s instructions.At trial, the adviser was asked whether the family’s concerns should have been escalated to a supervisor or the firm’s risk-management team. “Sure. It should have been,” Privitelli answered, according to the court’s account of the testimony.The family alleged that Morgan Stanley and Privitelli should have taken greater steps to assess the risks of continuing the trading strategy. They also challenged advice they said the adviser provided on tax and estate-planning matters, claiming it contributed to expensive insurance arrangements and tax liabilities.The defendants disputed the allegations. The case therefore centres not simply on how much money Voce made or lost, but on what the financial professionals knew about his circumstances and what responsibilities they had towards him.The family first pursued arbitration through the Financial Industry Regulatory Authority, or FINRA, in 2014. A panel dismissed the claims in January 2019, without prejudice to the family pursuing them in court. The family filed a lawsuit in Los Angeles County Superior Court in April 2019. During the 2024 trial, the court ruled that the claims were timely but restricted the conduct for which the family could seek damages to the period after September 11, 2010.The trial court subsequently dismissed the financial elder abuse claim, reasoning that the investment accounts had increased in value during the relevant period. The defendants pointed to approximately $4.2 million in net gains from 2010 to 2012. The court also dismissed the excessive-trading theory of the fiduciary-duty claim, finding that the family had not presented sufficient expert evidence to establish that the trading volume or commissions were excessive.The family challenged those decisions, arguing that the lower court had wrongly excluded much of the investment relationship from consideration and placed too much emphasis on the account’s eventual performance. The appeals court agreed on key points. It held that once a claim is found timely, the statute of limitations does not automatically restrict the family to recovering damages for only a narrow period of the alleged conduct.It also rejected the idea that an account’s gains, by themselves, defeated the financial elder abuse claim. Under California law, the court explained, the question includes whether a defendant knew or should have known that the conduct was likely to harm an older person when it occurred.“Under the Elder Abuse Act, a defendant who exposes an elder to a foreseeable risk of harm does not escape liability merely because the risk did not materialize,” the opinion stated.The court also ruled that questions about whether Privitelli’s responsibilities extended to tax and estate-planning advice could not be resolved solely by noting that he had not been formally hired or paid for those services. The broader relationship, including the advice actually provided and the client’s reliance on the adviser, had to be considered.However, the appeals court upheld the dismissal of the separate excessive-trading theory of the fiduciary-duty claim because the family had not provided sufficient expert evidence to support it.The ruling now allows the surviving claims to return to further proceedings. For Voce’s family, the legal dispute over how his fortune was managed in his final years remains unresolved. For the court, the central question is whether the evidence supports the allegations under the applicable legal standards, not simply whether the investor’s accounts ultimately made money.
Article Summary: Maurice Voce began investing in the 1960s and trading stock options in the 1970s. He worked with financial adviser Joseph Privitelli in the 1980s, when the adviser was associated with Dean Witter Reynolds, a firm that later merged with Morgan Stanley. His Morgan Stanley accounts were valued at about $18 million at the time of his death. His investments included a portfolio focused on income- generating assets and a trading account used for buying and selling stock options.

Article Title: A Pennsylvania couple spent nearly six years fighting to add a drive-through to their 5-7-acre truck stop after officials refused permission, but an October 27 appeals ruling overturned the denial and
Article Text:
Representative Image (AI-generated)

A truck stop looking to expand its food service

Why township officials rejected the proposal

Appeals court identifies conflicting zoning rules

Judges recognise the proposal as a natural expansion

A drive-through window may seem like a small addition to an established convenience store, but for one Pennsylvania couple, getting permission to build one turned into a legal battle lasting nearly six years. Their proposal involved a 5-7-acre truck stop that already sold freshly prepared food and served motorists around the clock. However, local zoning officials refused permission, arguing that township regulations prohibited drive-through facilities at convenience stores.The dispute reached the Pennsylvania Commonwealth Court, which ruled on October 27, 2026, in Jyotsna Jivani and Anil Jivani v. East Lampeter Township Zoning Hearing Board and East Lampeter Township, according to the court opinion available on Justia. The court overturned the lower court's decision upholding the denial, finding conflicting provisions in the township's zoning ordinance. It also recognised the proposed facility as a natural expansion of the existing business and sent the case back to the zoning board for further proceedings.Jyotsna and Anil Jivani own a property at 2622 Lincoln Highway East in East Lampeter Township, Lancaster County. The approximately 5-7-acre site contains a convenience store, petrol station and truck stop operating as a lawful nonconforming use in an agricultural zoning district.The store operates 24 hours a day and includes food counters operated by Subway and Champ's Fried Chicken. Customers can purchase freshly prepared meals, while passenger vehicles and tractor-trailers use separate fuelling facilities.The couple wanted to add a drive-through window so customers could order and collect food without entering the store. The proposal was influenced partly by changing customer preferences during the COVID-19 pandemic, when some customers, particularly elderly people, were uncomfortable entering indoor spaces. During a December 2020 zoning board hearing, Anil Jivani explained that the franchise was insisting on curbside delivery or a pickup window. He argued that the facility would give existing customers another way to purchase food rather than introduce an entirely new business.The couple submitted their zoning permit application around October 2020. After the township denied it, they appealed to the East Lampeter Township Zoning Hearing Board in November 2020, seeking approval or, alternatively, a special exception or variance. Their proposal involved replacing an existing bus-passenger drop-off lane beside the store with drive-through lanes. The design included a nine-foot-wide lane that would divide into two lanes, allowing vehicles to bypass the queue when necessary.The facility would provide approximately 120 feet of queuing space, accommodating four cars before the ordering kiosk and four afterwards. Only passenger vehicles would be allowed to use it. The construction also required a 38-square-foot addition at the rear of the building, offset by removing an equivalent area near the front entrance. Consequently, there would be no net increase in the store's usable floor area.Township officials argued that the zoning ordinance prohibited drive-through facilities at convenience stores. The board accepted this interpretation and denied the application on January 14, 2021. The Lancaster County Court of Common Pleas upheld the decision on August 14, 2025.The Pennsylvania Commonwealth Court examined two provisions of the township's zoning ordinance. Section 2020 defined a convenience store as a retail establishment selling groceries and ready-to-eat food, but excluded businesses with drive-through facilities. However, Section 23200 contained specific provisions addressing drive-through service lanes at convenience stores, including requirements for vehicle queuing.The judges found that the two provisions contradicted each other. Under Section 603.1 of Pennsylvania's Municipalities Planning Code, ambiguities in zoning restrictions must be interpreted in favour of the property owner. The township's zoning officer had testified that the permissive language was left in the ordinance by mistake during a 2016 overhaul. However, the court found that the conflicting provisions created ambiguity and that state law required the matter to be resolved in favour of the property owners. It therefore concluded that the zoning rules did permit drive-through facilities at convenience stores.The court also considered whether the proposed drive-through represented a natural expansion of the couple's existing nonconforming business. It found that the facility would not fundamentally change the store's primary activity of selling retail goods and prepared food. Instead, it would provide another way for customers to access products already available inside.The judges considered the property's history, including a 1988 zoning decision recognising a fast-food restaurant as part of the approved use, with seating for 30 to 35 customers. They also noted that the proposed changes involved limited physical alterations, no increase in overall floor area or paved lot coverage, and the replacement of a largely unused bus drop-off area.On October 27, 2026, the Commonwealth Court reversed the lower court's order and remanded the case to the East Lampeter Township Zoning Hearing Board for further proceedings consistent with its opinion. The ruling is non-precedential and does not automatically grant final construction approval. However, it removes the legal basis for the original denial and gives the couple another opportunity to pursue their proposed drive-through after years of litigation.
Article Summary: Jyotsna and Anil Jivani own a property at 2622 Lincoln Highway East in East Lampeter Township, Lancaster County. The approximately 5-7-acre site contains a convenience store, petrol station and truck stop operating as a lawful nonconforming use in an agricultural zoning district. The couple wanted to add a drive-through window so customers could order and collect food without entering the store. Their proposal involved replacing an existing bus-passenger drop-off lane beside the store with drive- through lanes. The Pennsylvania Commonwealth Court overturned the lower court's decision upholding the denial.

Article Title: A North Carolina judge has blocked a farm owner’s plan to build a 2,500-seat amphitheater on Orange County farmland covered by a 187-acre conservation easement that a dairy family signed nearly 30 yea
Article Text:
How the conservation dispute began

A long-running dispute over development on protected farmland in North Carolina has taken a significant turn after a Superior Court judge ruled in favour of a conservation group seeking to stop a proposed outdoor amphitheater. The October 15 decision effectively ends the prospect of a jury trial in the case, although the farm owner still has the option to appeal. According to reporting by The News & Observer, alongside earlier coverage by WRAL and Chapelboro, the dispute centres on Union Grove Farm in Orange County, where plans for a 2,500-seat entertainment venue have raised questions about land-use restrictions and the legal protection of agricultural landscapes. Superior Court Judge John Morris granted summary judgment in favour of Triangle Land Conservancy (TLC), the nonprofit that has been fighting the proposed development. The ruling was issued on October 15, ahead of a jury trial scheduled for November. Morris did not provide a detailed explanation of his decision in the reported proceedings. Union Grove Farm owner Greg Bohlen has 30 days to challenge the ruling before the North Carolina Court of Appeals.The legal battle dates back to 1995, when Bob Nutter, the late owner of Maple View Dairy, entered into a 187-acre conservation easement with Triangle Land Conservancy. The agreement was designed to protect the property's agricultural productivity, open spaces and scenic character while restricting certain forms of construction and development.The Nutter family eventually sold the property, with Bohlen's companies and business partners acquiring the farm in 2021. The new owners subsequently established Union Grove Farm, focusing on regenerative agriculture and vineyard operations.Tensions escalated when the conservancy raised objections to three newly constructed roads crossing the protected land and the proposed amphitheater. In August 2025, TLC filed a lawsuit seeking to have the roads addressed and prevent the entertainment venue from being built. The organisation argued that the proposed development was inconsistent with the original conservation agreement, which was intended to protect the land in perpetuity.Why the amphitheater faced oppositionThe dispute also involved Orange County's rules governing agritourism, which allow qualifying farms to conduct certain public-facing activities without following standard county zoning requirements. However, in June 2025, the county's planning director determined that the proposed amphitheater did not qualify as an agritourism activity and could not proceed under that exemption. The decision also rejected plans for additional commercial facilities, including 10 cottages, a 40-room farm stay centre, event space and a restaurant.Bohlen initially challenged the planning director's decision but later withdrew his appeal before a scheduled Board of Adjustment hearing in October 2025. His legal team had indicated that the farm could explore a revised proposal with a smaller venue and different activities. That development did not resolve the separate conservation dispute. TLC continued pursuing its lawsuit, seeking a legal determination that the amphitheater violated the easement regardless of how the project was classified under county regulations.The farm's future and what happens nextUnion Grove Farm has also defended its wider agricultural operations, which include muscadine grape cultivation, sheep grazing and vermiculture, a process that uses worms to turn organic waste into compost. Bohlen, a fifth-generation farmer who previously worked in venture capital, has promoted regenerative farming as a way to improve soil health and create a more sustainable agricultural ecosystem. The farm's operations extend across more than 1,200 acres in the Dairyland Road community.The latest ruling also dismissed a counterclaim brought by East-West Organics, an entity associated with the neighbouring Center for Regenerative Agriculture, which had sought clarification about possible future development on its property. The decision follows another setback for Bohlen in June 2026, when a separate counterclaim against Triangle Land Conservancy was dismissed. That case involved disagreements over whether Union Grove Farm, as a tenant, had the authority to renegotiate the original conservation agreement on behalf of the property owners.For now, the October ruling represents a major victory for Triangle Land Conservancy, which oversees more than 200 conservation easements across the region. The organisation has indicated that it supports the farm's regenerative agricultural work and hopes to work towards restoring the protected property's conservation values. However, the possibility of an appeal means the legal dispute may not be entirely over. The timeline for restoring the affected land and resolving the remaining disagreements has yet to be established.
Article Summary: The dispute centres on Union Grove Farm in Orange County, North Carolina. Plans for a 2,500-seat entertainment venue have raised questions about land-use restrictions and the legal protection of agricultural landscapes. Superior Court Judge John Morris granted summary judgment in favour of Triangle Land Conservancy on October 15.

Article Title: 'He was crying and grabbing the doctor's hands to stop him': US organ donation group faces decertification after Kentucky man’s near-fatal ordeal
Article Text:
Procedure stopped, but questions remained

Federal investigation identifies wider concerns

US authorities move to decertify Network for Hope

“My brother grabbed the doctor’s hand as he tried to harvest his organs…” Donna Rhorer’s account of what happened to her brother, Anthony Thomas “TJ” Hoover II, has become central to a case raising serious questions about patient safety and oversight in the US organ donation system. Hoover, who was taken for organ donation after a drug overdose in Kentucky in October 2021, showed signs of life as preparations for organ retrieval progressed. Nearly five years later, the case has drawn renewed scrutiny after US authorities moved to decertify Network for Hope, the organisation responsible for coordinating organ donations in the region.The US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) announced on August 5, 2026, that it had begun the process of decertifying Network for Hope following federal reviews that identified concerning patient-safety practices in multiple cases involving potential organ donors. Rhorer described her experience in testimony at the Kentucky Attorney General’s office, recounting how her family had been told that Hoover had no reflexes or brain activity and would not recover. They agreed to withdraw life support and honour his wishes to become an organ donor. However, she said, his behaviour during the subsequent preparations raised questions about whether he was still alive.“I was there, I saw what happened to my brother. They prepared to recover his organs while he was still alive.During that honour walk his eyes were open, he was tracking me and they told me it was just reflex,” Rhorer testified.“And then during the heart cath, he was thrashing, crying and grabbing the doctor's hands to stop him. Even after those signs the organ procurement continued until the physician refused to proceed.”Rhorer also alleged that a coordinator contacted the organisation’s home office after the doctor refused to continue, only to be told to find another surgeon or risk losing her job. “One of the organisation’s own coordinators called the home office after the doctor refused, she was told, ‘find another surgeon or you'll lose your job because we're finishing this case. My brother almost died that day, that should never happen to anyone. Laws and standards were clearly violated, those responsible must be held accountable,” she said.When the procedure was stopped, Rhorer said, the family was told to take Hoover home and make him comfortable because he was not expected to survive much longer.“Well, it's been five years, and he's still here. I'm grateful every day for that but he is not the same, he has nightmares, he struggles remembering things and he asked me 'sis, why do they wanna kill me?' I don't have an answer for him,” she said.Hoover’s case came to wider public attention in October 2024, when NPR reported accounts from witnesses who said he had shown signs of life during preparations for organ recovery. The Guardian also reported on the incident, including the concerns raised by former employees of the Kentucky Organ Donor Affiliates (KODA), the organisation now known as Network for Hope.Former KODA employee Nyckoletta Martin and organ-preservationist Natasha Miller raised concerns about Hoover’s condition. Miller, whose work involved preserving organs after removal, reportedly witnessed Hoover thrashing and crying on the operating table. Other accounts described him moving his head and pulling his knees towards his chest.The organ retrieval was ultimately stopped after a physician refused to proceed. Rhorer said the family was not initially given a full explanation of what had happened. She later learned more about the incident after a former KODA employee contacted her in January 2024.Hoover survived, but his family has described lasting difficulties with memory and other aspects of his daily life. Rhorer’s account has since become part of a wider debate over the responsibilities of organ procurement organisations (OPOs), which coordinate donations between hospitals, potential donors and transplant centres.The controversy intensified after federal authorities examined hundreds of cases handled by Network for Hope. In its August 5, 2026 announcement, HHS said the Health Resources and Services Administration had reviewed 351 cases between 2021 and 2024 in which organ donation had been authorised but ultimately did not proceed.Of those cases, 103 had concerning features, according to the department. It said 73 patients displayed neurological signs incompatible with organ donation. The review raised concerns about neurological assessments, communication between medical teams, consent practices and the classification of causes of death, particularly in cases involving drug overdoses.The findings do not mean that organs were removed from all the patients reviewed. Instead, they point to concerns about the assessments and preparations undertaken before donation could proceed. Organ recovery must follow the applicable medical and legal requirements for determining death.Following the federal review, HHS said Network for Hope had failed to demonstrate sufficient improvement despite earlier corrective measures and monitoring. Authorities therefore began the process of decertifying the organisation, which coordinates organ procurement across Kentucky and parts of Indiana, Ohio and West Virginia.The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services issued a notice stating that its Medicare agreement with Network for Hope would be terminated on November 3, 2026, subject to the applicable process. The organisation’s donation service area is expected to be transferred through a process that depends on the outcome of any appeal or the organisation’s decision not to appeal.Network for Hope has disputed aspects of the allegations and maintained that organ procurement organisations do not provide patient care or independently declare death. The organisation has also said that organ recovery can proceed only after an independent healthcare provider has declared a patient dead.The regulatory action has placed renewed focus on how hospitals and organ procurement organisations communicate with families, assess neurological activity and respond when relatives or medical staff raise concerns about a patient’s condition.The United States has more than 100,000 people waiting for organ transplants, making public confidence in the donation system critical. Experts and transplant advocates have stressed the importance of investigating alleged failures thoroughly while ensuring that individual cases do not discourage people from donating organs that could save lives.For Rhorer, however, the issue remains deeply personal. Her brother survived the procedure that was meant to lead to organ recovery, but she says he continues to live with the consequences of what happened. His case has now become part of a wider examination of patient safety and accountability in the US organ donation system.
Article Summary: Anthony Thomas 'TJ' Hoover II was taken for organ donation after a drug overdose in Kentucky in October 2021. He showed signs of life as preparations for organ retrieval progressed. Nearly five years later, the case has drawn renewed scrutiny after US authorities moved to decertify Network for Hope, the organisation responsible for coordinating organ donations.

Article Title: Indian national pleads guilty to $227-million medicare fraud in US over fake Covid-19 test kit claims
Article Text:
Syed Murtuza Kablazada pleads guilty to 227 million medicare fraud scheme.

An Indian national has pleaded guilty in the US to two counts of health care fraud for his role in a $227 million scheme that used the personal information of hundreds of thousands of Medicare beneficiaries to submit false claims for COVID-19 test kits.Syed Murtuza Kablazada, 36, who lived in Des Plaines, Illinois, caused three Chicago-area laboratories to bill Medicare for test kits that beneficiaries had neither requested nor received, according to the US Department of Justice (DOJ).Court documents show that Kablazada and his co-conspirators acquired three laboratories, Chicago Care, V Care and Al-Ameer, over six months beginning in January 2023.They then paid approximately $11 million to a telemarketing company based in Pakistan to obtain personally identifiable information belonging to hundreds of thousands of Medicare beneficiaries. The information was used to submit fraudulent claims worth $227 million for COVID-19 test kits.Medicare paid approximately $136 million against those claims, although the kits were never requested by or shipped to the beneficiaries, the DOJ said.Investigators said Kablazada and his associates used overseas money transfers and unlicensed money transmitters to conceal their involvement and distribute the proceeds. Some of the money was used to purchase luxury vehicles.
Article Summary: Syed Murtuza Kablazada, 36, pleaded guilty to two counts of health care fraud. Used personal information of hundreds of thousands of Medicare beneficiaries to submit false claims for COVID-19 test kits. Some of the money was used to purchase luxury vehicles.

Article Title: 'I'm not broken...': At 21, he survived burns on 85% of his body after a gas explosion, years later he prepares school lunches for hundreds of students while building his dream life
Article Text:
A gas explosion changed his life forever

Finding a family when he needed one

The people who helped him find work

A home of his own and a beagle named Snoopy

At 21, Joey Brown survived a gas explosion that left burns across 85% of his body, beginning a long and painful journey of surgeries, rehabilitation and learning to perform everyday tasks again. Decades later, he is rebuilding his life in a Georgia high school cafeteria, where he helps care for hundreds of students and has found a community that believes in him. Now, as he looks towards owning a home and welcoming a beagle named Snoopy, Brown says he no longer sees himself as a broken man.A report published by CBS Atlanta documented how Brown, who works at Central High School in Carrollton, Georgia, found renewed purpose through employment and the support of his church. The Georgia Vocational Rehabilitation Agency (GVRA), which helped him secure the job, had previously detailed the long road that brought him back into the workforce.In 1988, Brown had recently moved out of his parents’ home and was sharing an apartment with his brother in Winter Garden, Florida. According to GVRA, he was watching an Atlanta Braves baseball game when he lit a cigarette. The flame ignited fumes from a gas leak, triggering an explosion that knocked him unconscious.When Brown regained consciousness in the apartment complex’s parking lot, a police officer was standing over him and help was on the way. He was airlifted to a hospital in Orlando, where doctors determined that he had sustained severe burns across 85% of his body.The injuries would change nearly every aspect of his life. Brown eventually lost his left arm at the elbow and was left with four fingers on his right hand. His recovery involved repeated operations and a prolonged hospital stay. “I’ve had probably 30 to 50 surgeries over the years,” Brown told CBS Atlanta. “I was in the hospital for two and a half years. I had to learn how to walk again and feed myself again.”The physical injuries were only part of the struggle. For years, Brown found it difficult to face the outside world, conscious of the scars that made strangers stare at him. “For a long time, I hid from the world. And because of my burns and scars, people would stare at me. But it doesn’t bother me no more,” he told CBS Atlanta.Brown’s journey back to independence was not something he managed alone. His faith and his involvement with Midway Church in Villa Rica, Georgia, helped him build relationships and find a sense of belonging. He became a greeter at the church, where his willingness to encourage others made him an important presence in the community. Members came to know him not simply as a man who had survived a devastating accident, but as someone who continued to offer kindness despite his own difficulties.“He is a great, great encourager to many, many people, and they depend on that,” Kay Thompson of Midway Church told CBS Atlanta. Brown said the relationships he developed at church helped fill a deeply felt absence in his life.“I prayed a long time for my own family, and Jesus showed me families every week to come and see me and visit me,” he said. It was through this community that Brown began working towards another milestone: finding a permanent job and becoming more independent.According to GVRA, Brown first approached the agency for assistance in 2020, but his case did not progress at that time. With encouragement from church member Gerry Herlugson, he reapplied in March 2024 and began receiving vocational rehabilitation services. The agency connected him with Wiregrass Resource Group, a supported-employment organisation, where Kehli Pope became his job coach. Together, they worked towards finding an employer willing to give Brown an opportunity.One unexpected obstacle was the fingerprint-based background check required for school employment. Brown no longer had fingerprints because of his injuries. Pope contacted the school system and helped secure acceptance of a doctor’s note explaining his condition.She also helped him adjust to his responsibilities in the cafeteria, drawing on skills he had already developed while washing dishes at church. “He washes dishes like a pro,” Pope told GVRA.Brown’s work at Central High School includes operating the commercial dishwasher, disposing of rubbish and helping clean his coworkers’ workstations. After the school year ended in May 2026, he also took a position as an aide in the district’s summer meal programme. His coworkers have welcomed him as one of their own. Beana Nolley, who works alongside him, told CBS Atlanta that Brown brings energy and warmth to the kitchen. “Mr. Joey lights up our kitchen,” she said.Nolley also described how students notice Brown working despite having one arm, using his example to encourage them to believe in their own abilities. For Brown, the job has brought something he had struggled to find after years of uncertainty: a reason to look forward to the next day.“It makes me look forward to tomorrow because I didn’t have nothing to look forward to and give myself hope. And now I got hope from having a job again,” he told CBS Atlanta.With employment providing greater stability, Brown has begun looking beyond simply getting through each day. His next goal is to own a home, where he can live more independently and welcome a dog of his own. GVRA reported in July that Brown had been living with his sister for 14 years and hoped to purchase his first home by December 2026. He has been saving towards that goal, while Herlugson has organised a separate fundraiser to help with the down payment.Brown already knows what he wants to call his future companion. “I want to be in my own home by December, so I can celebrate Christmas with my new puppy. My puppy is a beagle. I have decided to name him Snoopy,” he told GVRA.Church members have offered to contribute their time, labour and, in some cases, building materials to help him achieve his dream. Herlugson told CBS Atlanta that the project had become a shared goal for the community.After years in which his injuries and scars shaped how he saw himself, Brown is now looking towards a future defined by his own choices. “I was a broken man now, and I’m not broken no more,” he told CBS Atlanta.For Brown, the dream is not simply about a house or a puppy. It is about the independence, belonging and everyday happiness he spent years trying to regain, and the people who helped him believe those things were still possible.
Article Summary: Joey Brown lost his left arm at the elbow and was left with four fingers on his right hand after a gas explosion left him with burns across 85% of his body. For years, Brown found it difficult to face the outside world, conscious of the scars that made strangers stare at him. His faith and his involvement with Midway Church in Villa Rica, Georgia, helped him build relationships and find a sense of belonging.

Article Title: Two Pennsylvania hunting clubs own 5,500 acres of private land; state Supreme Court ruling changes when game wardens can enter without a warrant
Article Text:
Representative Image of Clearfield County’s serene green fields and protected landscapes surrounding the Punxsutawney Hunting Club (AI-generated image)

Why the two hunting clubs challenged the Pennsylvania Game Commission

Open fields doctrine explained: what the Pennsylvania Supreme Court changed

What the justices agreed on, and where they differed

What the ruling means for landowners and game wardens

Two hunting clubs in Clearfield County, Pennsylvania, won a legal challenge over when government officials can enter private land without a warrant. On July 21, 2026, the Pennsylvania Supreme Court ruled 7-0 to overturn a 2007 precedent that had applied the federal open fields doctrine under the state constitution. The case involved the Punxsutawney Hunting Club, which owns 4,400 acres, and the Pitch Pine Hunting Club, which owns 1,100 acres. Represented by the Institute for Justice, the clubs argued that Pennsylvania’s constitution protects landowners who take sufficient steps to exclude intruders from their property. The court agreed that Article I, Section 8 provides broader protection than the Fourth Amendment in this context. However, the decision does not automatically protect every undeveloped property: its central holding concerns landowners who have demonstrated a reasonable expectation of privacy.The Punxsutawney and Pitch Pine hunting clubs own thousands of acres in Clearfield County. According to the Institute for Justice, which represented them, the properties are in the Allegheny Mountains region. The clubs posted no-trespassing signs, marked boundaries with purple paint, installed gates and fenced some areas to keep outsiders off their land.The dispute concerned the Pennsylvania Game Commission’s authority to enter private property while investigating potential hunting violations. According to the Pennsylvania Supreme Court’s opinion in Punxsutawney Hunting Club, Inc. v. Pennsylvania Game Commission, Game Commission officers entered the clubs’ land without consent, a warrant or probable cause at least 15 to 22 times since 2013. In one instance, a game warden placed a trail camera on Punxsutawney’s property, where it remained for 78 days, while investigating suspected illegal elk feeding.The clubs challenged provisions of the state’s Game and Wildlife Code that authorised officials to enter private property in the course of their duties. The case initially went before the Commonwealth Court of Pennsylvania. In September 2023, that court ruled against the clubs because it was bound by a 2007 state Supreme Court precedent, Commonwealth v. Russo. The clubs appealed, and the state Supreme Court heard oral arguments on April 9, 2025. The dispute ultimately turned on whether the state constitution protects an owner’s privacy interest in land beyond the immediate surroundings of a home or building, particularly when the owner has clearly marked the property as private.The open fields doctrine is a principle of US constitutional law under which undeveloped land outside the area immediately surrounding a home generally receives no protection from warrantless searches under the Fourth Amendment. In Hester v. United States in 1924, the US Supreme Court held that the Fourth Amendment’s protections did not extend to open fields. In Oliver v. United States in 1984, the court reaffirmed the doctrine, holding that fences and no-trespassing signs do not, by themselves, establish a reasonable expectation of privacy under the federal rule. Pennsylvania adopted a similar approach in Commonwealth v. Russo in 2007. In its July 21, 2026, ruling in Punxsutawney Hunting Club, Inc. v. Pennsylvania Game Commission, the state Supreme Court overruled Russo.Justice Kevin Brobson wrote the majority opinion. The court concluded that Article I, Section 8 of the Pennsylvania Constitution, which protects people in their persons, houses, papers and possessions, provides broader privacy protection than the Fourth Amendment in the context of open fields. The majority held that protection extends to private land beyond the immediate surroundings of a home or building when the owner has demonstrated a reasonable and legitimate expectation of privacy by taking sufficient steps to exclude intruders. Government officials must obtain a warrant based on probable cause or satisfy a recognised exception to the warrant requirement before entering land that meets this standard.The court struck down Sections 303(c) and 901(a)(2) of the Game and Wildlife Code as unconstitutional on their face because they authorised officials to enter private land without the necessary constitutional safeguards. The majority upheld Section 901(a)(8), which concerns administrative inspections, because nothing in the provision permits officers to enter private land, posted or otherwise.The justices were unanimous that Russo should be overruled and that Article I, Section 8 provides greater protection than the Fourth Amendment in this context. Their differences concerned the extent of that protection and the treatment of particular statutory provisions. Chief Justice Debra Todd joined the majority’s opinion except for its conclusion that Sections 303(c) and 901(a)(2) were unconstitutional on their face. She argued that the provisions could still be applied constitutionally to unposted land and should therefore be held unconstitutional only as applied to the hunting clubs’ posted properties.Justice David Wecht, joined by Justice McCaffery, agreed that the challenged entry provisions failed constitutional scrutiny but advanced a broader interpretation of privacy. He argued that a landowner’s reasonable expectation of privacy should not depend on signs, purple paint or fencing. He also disagreed with the majority’s decision to uphold Section 901(a)(8), the provision concerning administrative inspections. Justices Donohue and Mundy each wrote separate concurring opinions and joined the majority in full. Donohue wrote separately to stress that administrative searches remain available to the Game Commission. Mundy cautioned that greater state constitutional protection should never be presumed and that each request for such protection requires its own analysis. The majority left open whether landowners who had taken fewer steps to exclude intruders could also claim constitutional protection. It did not decide that every field, forest or rural property is protected regardless of how the owner has marked or controlled it.The decision changes the legal standard governing warrantless entry onto qualifying private land in Pennsylvania. It does not eliminate the Game Commission’s authority to enforce wildlife laws, nor does it invalidate every provision that permits inspections. For landowners, visible measures such as no-trespassing signs, boundary markings, gates and fencing may help establish a reasonable expectation of privacy. The ruling does not prescribe a universal checklist that guarantees protection in every case; whether the standard is met depends on the circumstances.For game wardens and other government officials, the decision means that their statutory enforcement responsibilities do not automatically authorise entry onto land protected by Article I, Section 8. They must obtain a warrant based on probable cause or rely on a recognised exception to the warrant requirement when entering property that meets the court’s standard. The Pennsylvania Game Commission said in its official response to the ruling that it was disappointed by the outcome but respected the court’s decision. It said its officers would continue protecting wildlife and enforcing hunting laws within the new constitutional standards.The Institute for Justice has argued that the decision has implications beyond the two clubs, including for other private landowners across Pennsylvania. The precise reach of the ruling will depend on how courts apply its standard to different properties and circumstances. The case establishes that, under Pennsylvania’s constitution, land beyond the immediate surroundings of a home can receive protection against warrantless government entry when the owner has demonstrated a reasonable expectation of privacy. It also leaves unresolved how that protection applies to landowners who have taken fewer steps to exclude intruders.
Article Summary: Two hunting clubs in Clearfield County, Pennsylvania, won a legal challenge over when government officials can enter private land without a warrant. On July 21, 2026, the Pennsylvania Supreme Court ruled 7-0 to overturn a 2007 precedent that had applied the federal open fields doctrine under the state constitution. The clubs argued that Pennsylvania’s constitution protects landowners who take sufficient steps to exclude intruders from their property. Government officials must obtain a warrant based on probable cause before entering land that meets this standard.

Article Title: 'Luckiest woman in history': Meet Joan Ginther, Stanford alumni who legally cheated lottery four times to win $20 million using mathematics and paper
Article Text:
Four wins, $20.4 million

Did a mathematics degree give her an advantage?

The mathematics behind scratch-off tickets

Winning a lottery jackpot once can change a person's life. Winning millions four times over 17 years, however, can turn even the most ordinary ticket into the subject of a mathematical mystery. Joan Ginther, an American with a doctorate in statistics from Stanford University, collected $20.4 million from four major Texas Lottery wins between 1993 and 2010. Her extraordinary record earned her the nickname “the luckiest woman on Earth” and fuelled speculation that she had discovered a way to improve her odds of winning.Ginther's story first attracted widespread attention in 2010, when she won a $10 million top prize from a $50 scratch-off ticket in Bishop, Texas. According to ABC News, the win was her fourth major lottery victory and brought her cumulative winnings to more than $20 million. What made the story particularly intriguing was her academic background: Ginther had earned a PhD from Stanford and had previously worked as a mathematics professor.Ginther's winning streak stretched across two types of lottery games: a conventional number-drawing game and instant scratch-off tickets.Her first major win came in 1993, when she received approximately $5.4 million as her share of an $11 million Lotto Texas jackpot. Thirteen years later, in 2006, she won $2 million in the Holiday Millionaire scratch-off game. In 2008, she collected another $3 million from a Millions & Millions scratch-off ticket. Her biggest prize arrived in 2010, when she won $10 million in the $140,000,000 Extreme Payout game.The Texas Lottery's official records confirm her 1993 jackpot claim, while its published milestones record her 2008 win and note that she became the first three-time Texas Lottery top-prize winner on record. ABC News reported her fourth major win in July 2010. The sequence was remarkable enough to attract national attention. But the details surrounding how Ginther selected her tickets remained largely unknown. She kept a low public profile, declined interview requests and did not explain her approach to playing the lottery.Ginther's academic background became central to speculation about her success. Her doctorate and experience teaching mathematics led some observers to wonder whether she had used probability theory, statistical analysis or knowledge of lottery games to identify more promising tickets. A 2011 Harper's Magazine investigation examined possible explanations for the repeated wins. The theories included access to inside information, mathematical skill and extraordinary luck. The investigation did not establish that Ginther had cheated or discovered a secret algorithm.A later investigation published through Philly.com, explored a more practical possibility: Texas made information about remaining prizes in scratch-off games publicly available. Could Ginther have used such data to identify games with better prospects? It suggested that the explanation might lie in the economics of scratch-off tickets rather than a mysterious formula. High-priced games can offer different prize structures and payout rates, while information about unclaimed prizes may help players compare available games. This investigation also identified numerous additional prizes claimed by Ginther and a friend, suggesting that the four headline wins did not tell the whole story of their lottery activity.Lottery tickets are not all identical in their prize structures. Scratch-off games have predetermined numbers of winning and losing tickets, and their advertised odds describe the probability of winning a prize under the game's rules. The chance of winning a top prize is different from the chance of winning any prize. A player who examines the remaining prizes in a game may be able to compare its published odds and potential returns with those of other games. Buying more tickets also increases the number of chances to win, although it increases spending and does not guarantee a profit.A 2024 paper in 'The College Mathematics Journal', titled 'The Luckiest Strategy on Earth? A Better Way to Buy Lottery Scratch-off Tickets', examined a strategy proposed in connection with Ginther's wins. Mathematician Skip Garibaldi analysed the approach using calculus and showed that the proposed strategy could improve expected returns compared with a naive approach. The research did not prove that Ginther used that strategy, nor did it demonstrate that she had reverse-engineered a lottery algorithm. Improving expected value in a particular game is not the same as guaranteeing a win, and the results cannot automatically be applied to every lottery.More than a decade after her final reported multimillion-dollar win, Ginther's strategy remains unconfirmed. Her story continues to fascinate lottery enthusiasts and mathematicians alike, not because it proves that the lottery can be beaten, but because it raises a question that has never been conclusively answered: was her success an extraordinary run of luck, a carefully informed approach to buying tickets, or some combination of the two?
Article Summary: Joan Ginther, an American with a doctorate in statistics from Stanford University, collected $20.4 million from four major Texas Lottery wins between 1993 and 2010. Her extraordinary record earned her the nickname ‘the luckiest woman on Earth’ The details surrounding how Ginther selected her tickets remained largely unknown.

Article Title: Arizona parents donated an adventure van to launch a charity inspired by their son’s rare disease; the organisation now reports $6.1 million in research grants to help tackle inherited blindness
Article Text:
A diagnosis that changed the family’s plans

How an adventure van became the first fundraiser

$5.1 million for experimental gene therapy

Expanding research beyond one condition

A fundraising model built around transparency

Poll Vote & Share your view What aspect of A Race Against Blindness do you find most admirable? Their transparency and accountability. Innovative fundraising strategies. Their commitment to research. Engagement with the community. 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

An Arizona couple turned a devastating diagnosis for their son into an unusual fundraising effort, donating a custom adventure van to launch a charity that says it has now paid out $6.1 million in research grants for inherited retinal diseases. According to A Race Against Blindness, founded by physician Stephen Johnston and his wife, nurse Kristina Johnston, the organisation grew out of their son Luke’s 2020 diagnosis with Bardet-Biedl syndrome, a rare genetic condition that can cause progressive vision loss. Its latest funding milestone includes $5.1 million committed to an experimental gene-therapy programme and $1 million for research into treatments that could benefit people with multiple inherited retinal conditions.The charity, which is registered as a US 501(c)(3) public organisation and is based in Gilbert, Arizona, says its aim is to accelerate research into diseases that can cause children to lose their sight. Its financial and grant history is available through its website, while its nonprofit registration and tax filings can be checked through ProPublica’s Nonprofit Explorer.In 2020, Luke was diagnosed with Bardet-Biedl syndrome (BBS), a genetic disorder that affects several parts of the body.Its symptoms can include retinal degeneration, obesity, kidney abnormalities and other complications, although their severity varies between individuals. The condition can cause retinitis pigmentosa, in which light-sensitive cells in the retina progressively deteriorate. Night vision may be affected first, followed by peripheral vision and, in some cases, substantial sight loss. The US National Library of Medicine’s MedlinePlus Genetics notes that BBS is associated with changes in several genes, including BBS1 and BBS10.For the Johnstons, the diagnosis brought uncertainty about what Luke’s future would look like and what could be done to protect his vision. Stephen Johnston, who is a physician, and Kristina Johnston, a nurse, said they were unfamiliar with the condition before their son’s diagnosis. They began looking into the research needed to develop treatments and concluded that funding was a major obstacle. Their response was to establish A Race Against Blindness, with the aim of supporting research while raising awareness of inherited retinal diseases that receive relatively little public attention.The organisation’s first major fundraising initiative began with a vehicle Stephen Johnston had purchased for his family. He donated the custom-built adventure van, made by 27North and valued at approximately $250,000, to serve as the grand prize in the charity’s inaugural sweepstakes.Rather than relying primarily on conventional fundraising dinners or events, the organisation used the prospect of winning a high-value vehicle to attract a wider audience. The idea was to reach people who might not otherwise encounter information about Bardet-Biedl syndrome or inherited blindness.According to the charity’s account, the first van fundraiser helped establish a model that it subsequently used for other vehicle and cash-prize campaigns. By the end of 2024, the organisation said it had paid out $3 million in research grants.A Race Against Blindness was recognised by the Internal Revenue Service as a tax-exempt public charity in February 2023. Its registration can be independently checked using its employer identification number, 92-2174042, through public nonprofit records.The charity’s largest funding effort has focused on AXV-101, an investigational gene therapy being developed by Axovia Therapeutics for Bardet-Biedl syndrome type 1, or BBS1. According to the organisation’s grant history, it awarded $1 million to Axovia in October 2024, followed by another $2 million in December that year. A further $1 million was awarded in September 2025, and $1.1 million in January 2026 brought its reported support for the programme to $5.1 million.The funding was intended to support the programme’s development, manufacturing, safety work and preparation for clinical testing. The charity says the money helped advance AXV-101 towards its first human clinical trial.Gene therapy seeks to address disease by introducing, replacing or modifying genetic material. In inherited retinal conditions, researchers are investigating whether such approaches can preserve or improve vision by targeting the underlying genetic defect. However, an investigational treatment is not the same as an approved therapy, and clinical studies are necessary to establish its safety and effectiveness. The AXV-101 programme is intended for people with BBS1-related disease. Its progress does not mean that a treatment or cure is available for all people with Bardet-Biedl syndrome.The charity’s work has also expanded beyond its original focus. In May 2026, it reported providing $60,000 to support the annual Bardet-Biedl syndrome conference, including patient travel and access to recorded sessions. In June, it announced a $1 million grant to the Foundation Fighting Blindness and the RD Fund for research into gene-agnostic therapies. The charity said a matching contribution brought the funding round’s total impact to $1.55 million.Unlike approaches designed for a particular genetic variant, gene-agnostic strategies aim to develop treatments that could potentially help people with different inherited retinal diseases. Such research may widen the range of conditions that can be addressed, although its eventual clinical benefits remain to be established. The organisation also launched a formal research-grants programme in 2026, publishing funding priorities and evaluation criteria for proposals.A Race Against Blindness says its sweepstakes are administered by American Sweepstakes & Promotion Co., an independent agency that conducts drawings and verifies winners. Its published rules provide a free mail-in entry option, meaning participants do not have to donate to enter. The charity also lists winners and makes annual financial reports available. ProPublica independently confirms the organisation’s nonprofit registration and provides access to its tax filings.The organisation’s mission remains closely tied to Luke’s diagnosis. What began with a family’s attempt to find options for their son has developed into a fundraising effort supporting research into inherited blindness more broadly.
Article Summary: A Race Against Blindness was founded by physician Stephen Johnston and his wife, nurse Kristina Johnston. The organisation grew out of their son Luke’s 2020 diagnosis with Bardet-Biedl syndrome, a rare genetic condition that can cause progressive vision loss. Its latest funding milestone includes $5.1 million committed to an experimental gene-therapy programme and $1 million for research into treatments for multiple inherited retinal conditions.

Article Title: In 2019, a Florida homeowner disputed her insurer's water-damage payment; Supreme Court ruled a later notice law could not apply retroactively
Article Text:
Representative Image of a split scene showing a water-damaged house alongside a stack of legal documents (AI-generated image)

Florida water-damage claim dispute: How the Rebecca Hughes case reached the Supreme Court

Why the Florida Supreme Court rejected retroactive application

What the ruling means for Florida property insurance policyholders

A Florida homeowner’s dispute over a water-damage payment has clarified when a state law requiring notice before suing a property insurer applies. On October 22, 2026, the Florida Supreme Court ruled that the presuit-notice requirement introduced in 2021 cannot be applied retroactively to property insurance policies issued before the law took effect. The case involved Rebecca Hughes, whose homeowners policy with Universal Property & Casualty Insurance Company ran from April 24, 2019, to April 24, 2020. After disputing the insurer’s payment for water damage, Hughes sued in August 2021 without giving the notice required under the new law. The trial court dismissed her complaint, but the Sixth District Court of Appeal reversed. In Universal Property & Casualty Insurance Company v. Rebecca Hughes, No. SC2024-0025 (Fla. Oct. 22, 2026), the Supreme Court approved the Sixth District’s decision and rejected a conflicting ruling from the Fourth District. All 7 justices agreed with the outcome, with Justice Tanenbaum writing a separate concurring opinion.Hughes held a homeowners insurance policy with Universal from April 24, 2019, to April 24, 2020. On May 29, 2019, she filed a claim for water damage.Universal reviewed the claim and made a payment, but Hughes considered the amount insufficient. She obtained 3 repair bids and sought additional payment from the insurer, according to the Florida Supreme Court’s opinion. On July 1, 2021, section 627.70152 of the Florida Statutes took effect as part of a broader overhaul of property insurance law. The statute covers lawsuits arising under residential or commercial property insurance policies, subject to its terms and exceptions. It introduced a requirement for claimants to give the Florida Department of Financial Services written notice of their intention to sue at least 10 business days before filing a lawsuit. Under subsection (5), a court must dismiss without prejudice a suit involving a claim for which the required notice was not given. A dismissal without prejudice does not, by itself, prevent the claimant from bringing the case again.On August 4, 2021, Hughes sued Universal over the disputed payment without submitting the new notice. Universal asked the trial court to dismiss her complaint, arguing that the notice requirement applied. The trial court agreed and dismissed the case without prejudice. Hughes appealed, and Florida’s Sixth District Court of Appeal reversed the dismissal. The dispute reached the state’s highest court to resolve a conflict among the district appeals courts over whether the new requirement applied to policies issued before July 1, 2021.In Cole v. Universal Property & Casualty Insurance Co., 363 So. 3d 1089 (Fla. 4th DCA 2023), the Fourth District had concluded that the notice requirement applied retroactively to existing policies. The Third District later adopted that interpretation in a separate case, while the First, Second, Fifth and Sixth Districts concluded that the statute did not apply retroactively. The Supreme Court heard oral arguments in Hughes’s case on February 5, 2025. The recording is available through The Florida Channel.Chief Justice Couriel authored the majority opinion. The court examined whether the Florida Legislature had clearly stated that section 627.70152 should apply to policies issued before July 1, 2021. Under the court’s established two-step test, it first looks for a clear legislative intention to make a law retroactive. Only if that intention is established does it consider whether retroactive application would violate constitutional principles. The court found no clear command in the statute. It considered the phrase “all suits” in section 627.70152(1), which describes the lawsuits covered by the provision, but concluded that the wording did not establish that the law extended to suits involving policies issued before its effective date.The court also rejected the Fourth District’s reasoning that the Legislature would have expressly excluded older policies if it intended the law to apply only to newer ones. According to the Supreme Court, the absence of language limiting a statute to future policies does not amount to clear evidence that lawmakers intended it to apply retroactively. The statute’s stated effective date also weighed against applying it to earlier policies. Universal argued that the notice requirement was procedural rather than substantive. The court disagreed after considering the law as a whole. The provision did more than establish a filing procedure: it delayed an insured’s ability to sue and gave insurers an additional opportunity to evaluate and pay claims before litigation. It also prescribed dismissal for noncompliance and, under subsection (8)(b), restricted recovery of attorney fees incurred before dismissal. That fee provision was subsequently repealed in 2022. The court concluded that these effects altered the rights and obligations of policyholders and insurers under property insurance contracts. It therefore declined to apply the notice requirement to Hughes’s 2019 policy.The key date is when the policy was issued, rather than simply when the damage occurred or when a lawsuit was filed. The Supreme Court held that section 627.70152’s presuit-notice requirement does not apply retroactively to policies issued before the provision took effect on July 1, 2021. Because Hughes’s policy was issued in April 2019, her lawsuit could not be dismissed for failing to comply with that later requirement. The ruling does not eliminate the pre-suit notice requirement for all property insurance lawsuits. The requirement remains applicable to policies issued on or after July 1, 2021, subject to the statute’s terms and exceptions. The decision addresses policies issued before that date and does not resolve the underlying dispute over whether Universal paid Hughes the correct amount for her water damage.Justice Tanenbaum wrote separately, concurring with the outcome but offering a different legal rationale. He pointed to section 624.21 of the Florida Statutes, which provides that amendments to the Insurance Code operate prospectively unless a contrary legislative intention is specified. In his view, that provision independently supported applying the notice requirement only prospectively because the Legislature had not expressly directed retroactive application.The Supreme Court approved the Sixth District’s decision in Hughes to the extent it was consistent with the opinion and disapproved the Fourth District’s contrary decision in Cole. That resolved the conflict among Florida’s district appeals courts over the reach of the 2021 notice requirement. The opinion states that it is not final until the period for filing a motion for rehearing expires and any timely motion is decided. The ruling does not determine whether Hughes is ultimately entitled to a larger insurance payment; it establishes that the 2021 pre-suit notice requirement cannot be used retroactively to dismiss her lawsuit over a policy issued in 2019.
Article Summary: Florida Supreme Court ruled that the presuit-notice requirement introduced in 2021 cannot be applied retroactively to property insurance policies issued before the law took effect. The case involved Rebecca Hughes, whose homeowners policy with Universal Property & Casualty Insurance Company ran from April 24, 2019, to April 25, 2020. After disputing the insurer’s payment for water damage, Hughes sued in August 2021.

Article Title: A Wyoming woman wanted to keep her miniature goat as a pet; a dispute over a local livestock ban became a constitutional lawsuit
Article Text:
Venus Bontadelli claimed that the city’s decision violated her constitutional rights. Image Credit: Courtesy Venus Bontadelli/Cowboy State Daily

How did a Wyoming woman’s pet goat lead to a constitutional lawsuit

The city’s permit rules became the centre of the dispute

Why did the dispute raise constitutional concerns

What happened to Porsche Lane during the legal battle

A settlement allowed the goat to return home

A Wyoming woman’s attempt to keep her miniature goat at home became a legal dispute over local animal regulations, the fairness of government decisions and constitutional rights. Venus Bontadelli, a resident of Powell, challenged the city’s permit process after officials refused to let her keep the animal as a pet. The disagreement raised questions about how local authorities classify companion animals and whether residents receive a fair opportunity to seek exceptions to restrictions. In January 2026, a settlement allowed the goat to return home, ending the immediate dispute without a court ruling on the constitutional claims.The case centred on Porsche Lane, a pygmy goat weighing about 20 pounds that had become part of the Bontadelli family. According to Wyoming Public Media, the goat was given to the family as a graduation present for their teenage daughter. She had been bottle-fed and raised as a companion animal.Bontadelli wanted to keep Porsche Lane at her home in Powell, but the city’s rules restricted livestock in residential areas.The family’s attempt to obtain permission through an exotic pet permit application became the starting point of the dispute.The Pacific Legal Foundation, which represented Bontadelli, argued that the city’s process was unfair. The organisation maintained that residents should have clear standards explaining when permission to keep an animal can be granted, rather than having applications depend on officials’ discretion.The disagreement was about more than whether a goat belonged in a residential neighbourhood. It also raised questions about how local governments make decisions affecting residents and whether their procedures provide adequate protection against arbitrary treatment.Pacific Legal Foundation argued that the city’s approach made it difficult for residents to understand what they needed to demonstrate to receive approval.Local authorities can regulate animals in residential areas to address concerns such as public health, neighbourhood conditions and the potential problems associated with livestock. However, disputes can arise when a resident believes a regulation has been applied unfairly or when the process for obtaining an exception lacks clear requirements.Bontadelli viewed Porsche Lane as a household pet rather than an animal kept for agricultural purposes. The city’s restrictions created a conflict between that understanding and the rules governing which animals residents could keep.Cowboy State Daily reported that Bontadelli had sued Powell over the decision. Its coverage described her efforts to keep the goat and the legal challenge arising from the city’s restrictions.The dispute demonstrated how the classification of an animal can have practical consequences for its owner. Even a small goat raised for companionship may fall under rules intended to regulate livestock, leaving residents to seek permission from their local government.The Pacific Legal Foundation filed the lawsuit in the US District Court for the District of Wyoming in November 2025. Its complaint argued that Powell’s ordinance violated the constitutional right to due process because the permit process did not provide sufficiently clear standards for deciding applications.Due process is a constitutional protection intended to ensure fairness in government procedures. In this case, the legal challenge focused on whether the city had established clear criteria governing who could receive permission to keep an otherwise restricted animal.The foundation argued that residents should not have to rely on uncertain or inconsistent decisions when seeking approval. Although cities have authority to establish rules for residential areas, those rules can be challenged when residents believe the procedures used to enforce them are constitutionally unfair.The lawsuit did not, however, result in a final judicial decision on those arguments. The case was resolved through a settlement before the court issued a ruling on the constitutional claims.While the dispute continued, the family could not keep the goat at home. Wyoming Public Media reported that Porsche Lane had been sent to California to stay with a friend after the city refused permission for the animal to remain in Powell.The separation made the disagreement a personal matter for the family, which had raised the goat as a companion animal. Bontadelli’s case also attracted attention because it involved a relatively small pet rather than livestock kept for commercial purposes.According to the report, the city council rejected the family’s appeal. Concerns were also raised about whether allowing the application could lead to more residents keeping goats within city limits.In a press release published on 14 January 2026, the Pacific Legal Foundation announced that Powell had agreed to issue Bontadelli a permit allowing Porsche Lane to return to the family. The settlement provided a practical resolution without requiring the court to decide whether the city’s rules were unconstitutional.The legal dispute had therefore achieved its immediate objective, although the settlement did not establish a general right for other Powell residents to keep miniature goats.
Article Summary: Venus Bontadelli challenged the city’s permit process after officials refused to let her keep the animal as a pet. The dispute raised questions about how local authorities classify companion animals and whether residents receive a fair opportunity to seek exceptions to restrictions. A settlement allowed the goat to return home, ending the immediate dispute without a court ruling on the constitutional claims.

Article Title: In 2019, South Carolina sank a 95-foot retired tugboat 30 miles off Georgetown; it joined a deepwater reef known for snapper, grouper and other fish
Article Text:
AI-generated representative image of a retired tugboat resting on the ocean floor, now serving as an artificial reef for marine life. Image credits: ChatGPT

The transition from a working tugboat to an artificial reef

Why South Carolina builds artificial reefs

A representative image of a tugboat. Image credits: Wikimedia Commons

Preparing retired vessels for deployment

On June 28, 2019, a retired 95-foot tugboat named Susan Richards was intentionally sunk in the Atlantic Ocean off South Carolina. The Department of Natural Resources (SCDNR) deployed the vessel at Vermilion Reef, an artificial reef site approximately 30 miles offshore from Georgetown. On July 3, SCDNR announced the deployment while describing the tugboat as another addition to the state’s artificial reef programme.The Susan Richards had served a different purpose in the same coastal waters prior to its retirement. According to the department’s FY2019 annual report , the tugboat had towed numerous barge-loads of material to artificial reef sites along the South Carolina coast. This deployment transformed a vessel that was previously used in the construction of underwater habitats into an artificial reef structure itself.Due to unfavourable weather conditions, the sinking had been postponed for several weeks. Ultimately, on June 28, conditions were favourable enough for the operation to proceed. After deployment, the tugboat came to lie at approximately 120 feet underwater at artificial reef site PA-17, popularly known as Vermilion Reef. Though there are no physical surface buoys marking the location, the exact location of the site is published by the SCDNR for boaters, anglers and divers.Sand covers much of South Carolina’s continental shelf, thus leaving relatively little naturally occurring hard-bottom habitats where reef communities might develop. The department reported that only about 5 to 10% of the seafloor has the geological characteristics needed to support these communities. Natural hard-bottom areas provide surfaces where organisms like sponges, corals and other invertebrates can attach and grow. Suitable hard surfaces in otherwise sandy areas are added by artificial reefs, thus expanding the habitat available to marine life.These artificial structures, however, do not become mature reef communities immediately after submersion. Instead, over time their surfaces get colonised by algae, barnacles, sponges, corals, hydroids, bryozoans and marine worms. These organisms form the foundation of the developing reef community and contribute to its food web. Apart from this, crabs, shrimps, sea urchins and small fish may also gather around the structures for shelter and food. On the other hand, larger fish use these areas as breeding and feeding grounds.Examples of populations associated with South Carolina’s artificial reefs include red snapper, black sea bass, gag grouper and king mackerel. The 2019 SCDNR announcement shows that a range of fish species like grouper, jacks, triggerfish and Spanish hogfish are supported by the Vermilion Reef’s deeper offshore setting.Artificial reef material usually undergoes a cleaning process to ensure it is suitable for the environment before deployment. The state’s programme utilises different durable materials like steel and concrete structures, ships, tugboats, barges, military vehicles and subway cars.On the other hand, the Susan Richards project was funded through a partnership between SCDNR and the Coastal Conservation Association of South Carolina (CCA-SC). Additional support was provided from the revenue generated through saltwater fishing licence purchases. This particular placement was the programme’s ninth major artificial reef project completed in partnership with CCA-SC, thus reflecting the involvement of state conservation authorities and fishing organisations in expanding offshore habitat and recreational fishing opportunities.
Article Summary: A retired 95-foot tugboat named Susan Richards was intentionally sunk in the Atlantic Ocean off South Carolina. The Department of Natural Resources (SCDNR) deployed the vessel at Vermilion Reef, an artificial reef site approximately 30 miles offshore from Georgetown. The Susan Richards had served a different purpose in the same coastal waters prior to its retirement.

Article Title: A Vermont dam built in the early 1900s to feed a private trout pond was breached in 2011; crews removed its remains in 2018, reopening 87 miles of stream
Article Text:
AI-generated representative image of a creek with trout swimming past the rubble of a removed dam. Image credits: ChatGPT

A dam built for a private trout pond

Removing the concrete remnants in 2018

Trout fish swimming in a pond. Image credits: Wikimedia Commons

Reopening 87 miles to fish passage

A dam constructed in Vermont in the early 1900s to provide water to a private trout fishing pond eventually turned into an obstruction to fish movement while disrupting the natural flow of a stream. The Killooleet Dam, located on the Hancock Branch of the White River near Camp Killooleet, was damaged by back-to-back floods before Tropical Storm Irene breached it in August 2011. This destroyed most of the structure, but concrete remnants stayed in the waterway, thus constricting the channel and preventing the stream from accessing the floodplain along its northern bank. After seven years, the White River Partnership (WRP) and its partners removed those remaining materials and carried out further channel improvements. The project reopened 87 miles of stream to fish passage.The Killooleet Dam was actually constructed in the early 1900s to feed a private trout fishing pond. As per reports, the estate was associated with a trout fishing club before becoming the site of a summer camp. During the major 1927 flood, the dam was reportedly damaged. It was, however, subsequently rebuilt when the camp was established.Camp Killooleet was established by Margaret Bartlett and Toni Taylor in 1927, with the Seeger family later taking ownership of the property.The structure suffered further damage during the flooding in 2008. Another major breach was caused by Tropical Storm Irene in August 2011. While the dam was no longer intact, its concrete remains continued to block part of the Hancock Branch. Thus, the problem was not just the presence of an obsolete dam, but the effects of the damaged structure that remained in the waterbody. The 2015 Upper and Middle White River Watershed Corridor Plan listed the removal of the destroyed dam as a high-priority project. Additionally, it identified that there was a separate requirement to improve the Hancock Branch’s connection with its floodplain. The plan noted that remnants of the old concrete structure created a channel constriction, while the affected area lacked some of the features needed for a more stable and diverse stream channel.The WRP received funding to develop priority projects identified in the corridor plan in 2017. Kate Seeger, who owned the Camp Killooleet property, expressed interest in working with the partnership on dam removal and floodplain restoration. The engineering design to help move the work forward was funded by her.
